lines: You have the Python, the history, and the shell. Now: how a change gets merged and released.
Five minutes on review, tests, continuous integration, version numbers and pinned dependencies. The strip along the top marks where each step sits in the flow.
Deploying comes later in the course. All familiar? Swipe on.
Start with review, and its order matters. A reviewer takes the broad view first, then the design of the main part.
Big problems go back immediately, before anyone reads the details. Only then come functionality, complexity, tests and naming.
Style comments are labelled as nits, meaning the author may skip them. And approve when the change clearly improves the code, not when it is perfect.
Two habits keep it fast: small changes, around a hundred lines, and an answer within one working day.
A good test pins a bug in place. Read the output on screen: six tests run, and four are cases of one test with different inputs.
A fixture hands each test a fresh directory, so tests never share state.
The question to ask of every test is whether it fails when the code is broken. On the broken commit, four fail and two pass.
Look at which ones fail: only the padded inputs, which is exactly the bug. A test that passes on broken code proves nothing.
Continuous integration looks complicated, but it is one idea. The runner does not understand your tests. It understands exit codes.
Watch the chain on the left. Each box is a fresh shell, and the only thing it hands back is a number. Zero means go on.
Now the right hand chain. The second step exits with one, and the two boxes after it never run.
Make the job a required check and a red run blocks the merge. That is the whole gate.
Here is where the previous refresher bites. A step runs a pipeline, and the step names no shell.
So the runner picks its default, which stops on the first error but does not check every stage of a pipe.
The first command can't open its file and fails with a two. The later ones are happy with empty input.
Does the step pass or fail?
answer: A pipeline's status is its last command's, which succeeded, so the stop on error option never sees the failure at the front.
Name the shell explicitly and the stricter pipe option comes with it. Now the step fails with the two, which is what you wanted all along.

lines: A flaky test gives different verdicts on identical code. Look at the count: half of twenty runs fail.
This one compared the order of a set. Set order depends on a hash, and Python seeds that hash differently in every process.
Re running until green hides the cause and teaches the team to ignore red.
The fix is to remove the unspecified order, here by sorting before comparing.
A version number is a promise. Three parts: a fix bumps the last, a compatible addition bumps the middle.
Now the next release renames an output column.
Which version is it?
answer: Every reader that looks up the old column name breaks, and that is exactly what a major bump warns about. The others reset to zero.
A minor or patch bump would promise compatibility that is not there, and a released version must never change, so rebuilding it is not allowed.

lines: Now why an application should pin exactly. The requirements file says the package at one point four, with a loose rule that allows later versions.
Your laptop installed one point five last week. Today a new major version is out, with the renamed column.
What does a fresh CI run install?
answer: The new major version, and the app fails with a missing key error.
A loose rule admits every later version, so a clean machine picks up whatever is newest. Your laptop only worked because it was old.
An application should pin exactly, with a lock. That is the next step.

lines: A lock file freezes the whole tree. Every package, including the ones you never named, is pinned to an exact version and the checksum of the exact file.
With the strict install option, the installer takes those bytes or nothing: a changed file is refused.
The gate's own tools are locked the same way.
One caution. A lock repeats an installation exactly. It cannot tell you the installed code is right, so it freezes today's mistakes along with today's versions.
Eight things to keep. Review the design first and keep changes small. Pin a bug with a test that fails on broken code.
The gate is a chain of exit statuses. Know which shell runs your step. Fix flakiness at the cause. A version number is a promise. Pin dependencies exactly, with a lock.
Notice the limit of the gate: it checks whether the answer is right, not what that answer costs as the data grows.
Anything rusty? The prerequisites panel points to good places to refresh it. Otherwise, on to the last of the five refreshers: the notation for that cost, and the logarithms the chapter counts with.
